newsitem.title: GERMANY: No delay to German budget timetable - ministry.
newsitem.headline: No delay to German budget timetable - ministry.

text.p: Germany's Finance Ministry on Monday squashed talk in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition government that the passage of the 1997 budget might be delayed until early next year.
A ministry source said the budget should be put before parliament for a final vote towards the end of November. "We are sticking to the planned timetable," the source said.
Coalition sources had said earlier that the passage of the budget could be postponed to January.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has been battling to plug gaps in his finance plans, and last week came under renewed attack after Germany's six leading economic institutes said he would miss qualification targets for European monetary union.

The coalition is still discussing savings to bring Germany within the Maastricht treaty's budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product. The institutes predicted the 1997 deficit at 3.5 percent.

Also important for finalising the budget are parliamentary proceedings on finding a compromise over the 1997 tax bill -- parts of which had been blocked by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), which controls the upper house.

There are still outstanding elements in the tax bill which have not yet been agreed on -- including increasing personal tax allowances and compensating Germany's 16 states for the abolition of the wealth tax.

The Bundestag lower house of parliament is due to hold a final vote on the tax bill this Thursday, and the government wants the SPD-controlled Bundesrat to vote on the bill as soon as possible to enable the budget to be finalised, sources said.
